articles.title: Overcoming mixing challenges in high-viscosity bioprocesses
articles.text:
Articles Overcoming mixing challenges in high-viscosity bioprocesses As bioprocess intensification pushes cell densities higher, engineering the right agitation strategy becomes the critical factor separating productive runs from failed batches. Written by Erika Russell Erika Russell Erika Russell, BSc, is a Science Writer and Editor for LabX Media Group. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 5, 2026 | 6 min read Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses demands precise torque, agitation profiles, and impeller selection to maintain mass transfer and culture homogeneity. GEMINI (2026) Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 6:00 Highlights in this article Why viscosity is the hidden variable in intensified bioprocessing The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications CFD modeling as a scale-up tool for viscous bioprocesses Dissolved oxygen control strategies for viscous cultures Achieving consistent homogeneity in intensified bioreactor mixing Thicker, intensified cultures create bigger mass transfer problems, and only precise agitation keeps them in check. When cell densities climb and viscosity rises in fed-batch and perfusion processes, conventional mixing assumptions break down. Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses requires a fundamentally different engineering approach, one that accounts for torque limitations, oxygen transfer rates, and shear sensitivity simultaneously. Key takeaways High-viscosity bioprocesses alter fluid dynamics in ways that standard mixing models underestimate. Rising culture viscosity reduces bulk flow velocity and creates stagnant zones that impair nutrient distribution and oxygen transfer, directly threatening cell viability and product quality. Impeller selection and configuration are the primary levers for managing mixing in dense, viscous cultures. Radial-flow and axial-flow impellers each offer distinct trade-offs between shear stress, power consumption, and bulk blending efficiency that must be matched to the specific culture system. The kLa value (the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient) is the practical benchmark for mixing adequacy in high-viscosity systems. Engineering teams that monitor and optimize kLa across scale can predict and prevent the oxygen limitation events that derail intensified runs. Why viscosity is the hidden variable in intensified bioprocessing Process intensification strategies (including high-density fed-batch, concentrated feeding regimens, and N-1 perfusion seed trains using alternating tangential flow filtration ) consistently push cultures toward rheological conditions that standard bioreactor mixing designs were never optimized to handle. As viable cell densities reach 40 to 80 million cells per milliliter in intensified fed-batch and continuous processes, and as concentrated glucose feeds and accumulated metabolites thicken the culture broth, fluid behavior shifts from Newtonian toward non-Newtonian, meaning viscosity itself becomes a dynamic variable that changes with shear rate, temperature, and fermentation stage. This rheological shift has direct consequences for bioreactor mixing performance. Research published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering on non-Newtonian rheology in suspension cell cultures has demonstrated that assuming Newtonian viscosity significantly underpredicts shear stress in stirred bioreactors, and that shear stress values in high-density cultures can exceed those required to alter genetic expression in common cell lines. The Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow) drops as viscosity rises, pushing the flow regime from turbulent toward transitional or even laminar. Homogeneous mixing, which relies on turbulent energy dissipation to blend nutrients and disperse oxygen bubbles throughout the vessel, becomes increasingly difficult to sustain without either increasing impeller speed or redesigning the mixing geometry entirely. Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More The result is a set of competing engineering pressures that define the core challenge of mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses. Higher agitation speed increases power draw and shear stress, which can damage fragile cells or aggregates. Lower agitation preserves cell integrity but risks the formation of dead zones where oxygen depletion and nutrient gradients accumulate. The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Oxygen transfer rate (OTR) is the first parameter to deteriorate as culture viscosity rises. Oxygen is sparingly soluble in aqueous culture medium, and its transfer from the gas phase into the liquid phase depends on the gas-liquid interfacial area and the liquid film mass transfer coefficient. Both are adversely affected by increased viscosity. Higher viscosity suppresses bubble rise velocity, promotes bubble coalescence into larger low-surface-area bubbles, and reduces the turbulent eddies that thin the liquid film around each bubble, all of which decrease the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa). The relationship between kLa and viscosity is well characterized in published bioprocess engineering literature. A 2025 study in Biotechnology Journal on CHO cell suspension rheology and its effects on high-density cultivation found a 10 to 40% decrease in the volumetric mass transfer coefficient as culture rheology shifted from water-like conditions. This means that a bioreactor running an intensified process may require substantially more agitation power to maintain the same dissolved oxygen (DO) setpoint compared to a standard lower-density fed-batch in the same vessel. Carbon dioxide removal presents a parallel and frequently underappreciated mass transfer challenge in high-viscosity cultures. CO₂ accumulation is a known inhibitor of cell growth and a driver of pH excursions, and its stripping from viscous broth is governed by similar mass transfer physics as oxygen absorption. Engineers designing agitation strategies for high-density cultures must account for both gas transfer directions simultaneously, which often means optimizing sparger design and gas flow rates alongside impeller configuration. Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications The impeller is the primary tool for delivering mechanical energy to the culture and generating the fluid motion that drives mixing and mass transfer. For high-viscosity bioprocesses, impeller selection cannot default to the configurations used in standard fed-batch processes. The choice between radial-flow impellers, such as Rushton turbines, and axial-flow impellers, such as pitched-blade or hydrofoil designs, involves trade-offs that become more consequential as viscosity rises. Radial-flow impellers generate strong turbulence and high local shear in the impeller discharge zone, which benefits gas dispersion and kLa but creates steep shear gradients that can damage shear-sensitive cells. Axial-flow impellers produce lower local shear with better bulk circulation, which is advantageous for maintaining culture homogeneity in large-volume or high-viscosity systems where flow circulation is the limiting factor rather than local turbulence. Many modern bioreactor designs for intensified processes use staged impeller configurations, combining a radial-flow lower impeller for gas dispersion with one or more axial-flow upper impellers for bulk mixing. Published engineering guidance for animal cell culture places the standard D/T range between 0.33 and 0.5, and moving toward the upper end of that range can significantly improve mixing time and reduce zone heterogeneity in viscous cultures. As culture viscosity rises, torque demand increases nonlinearly, so the mechanical drive system must be specified with adequate torque capacity, validated against the worst-case viscosity expected at peak cell density before committing to a vessel configuration. CFD modeling as a scale-up tool for viscous bioprocesses Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has moved from a research tool into a practical engineering resource for bioreactor scale-up, and its value is particularly high for high-viscosity applications where empirical correlations developed for low-viscosity systems can mislead. CFD models solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion in three dimensions, accounting for the geometry of the vessel, impeller, and sparger, and can incorporate non-Newtonian rheological models to simulate the behavior of viscous culture broth. For bioreactor mixing challenges in high-viscosity processes, CFD modeling allows engineers to visualize flow fields, identify stagnant zones, and predict mixing times before a physical vessel is constructed or modified. Simulations of non-Newtonian fermentation broths can accurately predict mixing time increases relative to water-like conditions, with stagnant zone formation confirmable by tracer experiments in physical vessels. A mass-transfer modeling study in Biochemical Engineering Journal demonstrated that this approach enabled direct scale-up of a CHO antibody process from 2-L to 1,500-L without intermediate steps, with consistent process performance and product quality across scales. The practical workflow typically begins with rheological characterization of the culture broth, construction of a three-dimensional vessel geometry model, and simulation of fluid flow across a range of agitation speeds and gas flow rates. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start. Dissolved oxygen control strategies for viscous cultures Maintaining dissolved oxygen above the critical threshold becomes progressively more difficult as culture viscosity rises and kLa declines. Setpoints commonly fall in the range of 20 to 60% air saturation for mammalian cell cultures, with working targets often set between 30 and 50%. The standard dissolved oxygen control cascade, which increases agitation speed and then increases airflow rate as DO falls, remains the primary control strategy but must be implemented with culture-specific limits to prevent shear damage or excessive CO₂ accumulation from high gas flow rates. Oxygen enrichment of the inlet gas stream (substituting pure oxygen or high-oxygen mixtures for air) is a widely used supplemental strategy for maintaining DO in high-density, high-viscosity cultures. By increasing the partial pressure of oxygen in the sparged gas, enrichment increases the driving force for oxygen transfer across the gas-liquid interface without requiring a proportional increase in gas flow rate, which would otherwise strip CO₂ and drive pH excursions. Oxygen enrichment must be implemented carefully because elevated local oxygen concentrations near the sparger can cause oxidative stress in cells close to the bubble formation zone. Read More Microspargers (spargers with very small pore sizes that generate fine bubbles) increase the gas-liquid interfacial area and improve kLa in viscous cultures, but are more prone to fouling and require higher inlet pressure to overcome surface tension effects at the pore. Combining a microsparger for oxygen transfer with a ring sparger for CO₂ stripping is an approach used in some high-density culture systems to address both gas transfer directions independently. Achieving consistent homogeneity in intensified bioreactor mixing Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses is a system-level engineering challenge that requires integrating rheological characterization, impeller selection, drive system specification, dissolved oxygen control strategy, and CFD-guided scale-up into a coherent process development program. The teams that manage this challenge successfully treat mixing as a first-class process parameter from the earliest stages of intensified process design, rather than as a scale-up problem to be solved after the biological performance has been locked in. For programs moving toward commercial manufacturing, the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities provides a framework for integrating these mixing specifications into facility design from the outset. The increasing adoption of high-density fed-batch and continuous perfusion platforms, and the insights that connect those approaches to the wider discipline of bioprocessing scale-up , make high-viscosity mixing engineering a near-universal challenge for modern biomanufacturing. Investing in rigorous mixing characterization and physically validated CFD modeling during process development is the most reliable way to prevent agitation failures from appearing at commercial scale, where inadequate agitation means lost batches, failed DO control, and irreproducible scale-up. This article was produced under Drug Discovery News' AI Editorial Guidelines . Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses? Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses refers to the agitation strategies and engineering approaches used to maintain homogeneous culture conditions (including nutrient distribution, dissolved oxygen, and pH uniformity) when culture broth rheology departs from standard low-viscosity conditions due to high cell densities, concentrated feeds, or accumulated metabolites. Why does high cell density increase culture viscosity? Elevated cell density increases the volumetric fraction of suspended biomass in the culture medium and promotes the accumulation of extracellular proteins, polysaccharides, and metabolic byproducts that collectively raise apparent viscosity. Non-Newtonian rheological behavior emerges when these components interact with shear forces during agitation. How does viscosity affect oxygen mass transfer in bioreactors? Increased viscosity reduces the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa) by promoting bubble coalescence, slowing bubble rise velocity, and thickening the liquid film resistance at the gas-liquid interface. The result is impaired oxygen supply to cells, which risks dissolved oxygen limitation and reduced cell productivity. Jun 2, 2026 | 3 min read Whole-body magnetic particle imaging (MPI) enables quantitative, noninvasive tracking of injected therapeutic cells across tissues, allowing researchers to compare how different injection routes affect delivery to target organs. Miranda Ansari Download PDF Cell therapies have transformed treatment for certain blood cancers and hold promise for autoimmune diseases and neurological conditions, but they share a fundamental problem: once therapeutic cells are injected into a patient, clinicians have almost no way to know where they go. Conventional imaging technologies including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) cannot reliably visualize the small cell numbers involved in these treatments, leaving researchers without feedback on whether a therapy is reaching its target, how many cells arrive, or why some patients respond and others do not. A study published in Science Advances from researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine describes a potential path toward solving that problem. Using magnetic particle imaging (MPI) — a newer imaging technology that detects magnetically labeled cells with high sensitivity and no tissue background signal — the team tracked two types of therapeutic cells across the whole body in living mice, comparing how injection route, cell size, dose, and disease state influenced biodistribution. The results suggest MPI could eventually provide the real-time, quantitative cell tracking that cell therapy development has so far lacked. In a press release , senior author Jeff Bulte , professor of radiology and radiological science and director of cellular imaging at the Johns Hopkins Institute for Cell Engineering, said that the work points toward using MPI to determine more precise cell therapy doses for individual patients. Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More What the imaging revealed The team labeled two cell types of different sizes — mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) at approximately 25 micrometers and neural precursor cells (NPCs) derived from induced pluripotent stem cells at approximately 10 micrometers — with superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) nanoparticles, then injected them into normal mice and mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a well-established preclinical model for multiple sclerosis (MS). MPI generates a positive signal proportional to the number of labeled cells present and is not attenuated by surrounding tissue — unlike MRI, which produces hypointense signals prone to artifacts and interference. That quantitative, whole-body readout allowed the team to assess cell distribution across multiple organs simultaneously without ionizing radiation or sacrificing the animal. The most significant finding concerned delivery route. Intra-arterial injection resulted in substantially more cells reaching target organs — the brain and spleen — compared with intravenous injection. In EAE mice, therapeutic cells accumulated in the spleen, an organ implicated in MS pathology. In the press release, lead author Ali Shakeri-Zadeh , assistant professor of radiology and radiological science at Johns Hopkins, noted that the spleen is thought to be a source of harmful immune T cells in MS, and that the accumulation of therapeutic cells there suggested they could engage disease activity directly at that site. The imaging also revealed off-target accumulation in the lungs and liver — relevant for biodistribution safety assessments. In normal mice, cells traveled to the lungs, liver, and brain, but were not detectable in the spleen, underscoring that disease state shaped organ distribution in ways healthy animal data alone could not predict. Why this matters for cell therapy development Dosing decisions for cell therapies are currently made with limited information about how many cells actually reach the intended site, conflating variability in delivery with variability in response. A quantitative imaging readout that decouples the two would allow developers to optimize injection routes, refine dose ranges, and identify sources of variability that make cell therapy outcomes difficult to predict or replicate. Previous work established MPI's utility for tracking adoptively transferred T cells in vivo in brain tumor models, showing that magnetic labeling does not impair cell function and that MPI can detect labeled cells after intravenous or intracerebroventricular delivery. The Johns Hopkins study extends that precedent across a broader range of cell types, delivery routes, and disease contexts. Human-scale MPI systems capable of brain imaging have been developed and validated in recent literature. As the technology moves toward clinical application, preclinical datasets like those generated here will be critical for interpreting what human MPI images of therapeutic cell distribution actually mean — and whether real-time imaging at the point of delivery can move cell therapy dosing toward the individualized model precision medicine requires. Jun 2, 2026 | 3 min read Whole-body magnetic particle imaging (MPI) enables quantitative, noninvasive tracking of injected therapeutic cells across tissues, allowing researchers to compare how different injection routes affect delivery to target organs. Miranda Ansari Download PDF Cell therapies have transformed treatment for certain blood cancers and hold promise for autoimmune diseases and neurological conditions, but they share a fundamental problem: once therapeutic cells are injected into a patient, clinicians have almost no way to know where they go. Conventional imaging technologies including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) cannot reliably visualize the small cell numbers involved in these treatments, leaving researchers without feedback on whether a therapy is reaching its target, how many cells arrive, or why some patients respond and others do not. A study published in Science Advances from researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine describes a potential path toward solving that problem. Using magnetic particle imaging (MPI) — a newer imaging technology that detects magnetically labeled cells with high sensitivity and no tissue background signal — the team tracked two types of therapeutic cells across the whole body in living mice, comparing how injection route, cell size, dose, and disease state influenced biodistribution. The results suggest MPI could eventually provide the real-time, quantitative cell tracking that cell therapy development has so far lacked. In a press release , senior author Jeff Bulte , professor of radiology and radiological science and director of cellular imaging at the Johns Hopkins Institute for Cell Engineering, said that the work points toward using MPI to determine more precise cell therapy doses for individual patients. Read More What the imaging revealed The team labeled two cell types of different sizes — mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) at approximately 25 micrometers and neural precursor cells (NPCs) derived from induced pluripotent stem cells at approximately 10 micrometers — with superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) nanoparticles, then injected them into normal mice and mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a well-established preclinical model for multiple sclerosis (MS). MPI generates a positive signal proportional to the number of labeled cells present and is not attenuated by surrounding tissue — unlike MRI, which produces hypointense signals prone to artifacts and interference. That quantitative, whole-body readout allowed the team to assess cell distribution across multiple organs simultaneously without ionizing radiation or sacrificing the animal. The most significant finding concerned delivery route. Intra-arterial injection resulted in substantially more cells reaching target organs — the brain and spleen — compared with intravenous injection. In EAE mice, therapeutic cells accumulated in the spleen, an organ implicated in MS pathology. In the press release, lead author Ali Shakeri-Zadeh , assistant professor of radiology and radiological science at Johns Hopkins, noted that the spleen is thought to be a source of harmful immune T cells in MS, and that the accumulation of therapeutic cells there suggested they could engage disease activity directly at that site. The imaging also revealed off-target accumulation in the lungs and liver — relevant for biodistribution safety assessments. In normal mice, cells traveled to the lungs, liver, and brain, but were not detectable in the spleen, underscoring that disease state shaped organ distribution in ways healthy animal data alone could not predict. Why this matters for cell therapy development Dosing decisions for cell therapies are currently made with limited information about how many cells actually reach the intended site, conflating variability in delivery with variability in response. A quantitative imaging readout that decouples the two would allow developers to optimize injection routes, refine dose ranges, and identify sources of variability that make cell therapy outcomes difficult to predict or replicate. Previous work established MPI's utility for tracking adoptively transferred T cells in vivo in brain tumor models, showing that magnetic labeling does not impair cell function and that MPI can detect labeled cells after intravenous or intracerebroventricular delivery. The Johns Hopkins study extends that precedent across a broader range of cell types, delivery routes, and disease contexts. Human-scale MPI systems capable of brain imaging have been developed and validated in recent literature. As the technology moves toward clinical application, preclinical datasets like those generated here will be critical for interpreting what human MPI images of therapeutic cell distribution actually mean — and whether real-time imaging at the point of delivery can move cell therapy dosing toward the individualized model precision medicine requires. When cell densities climb and viscosity rises in fed-batch and perfusion processes, conventional mixing assumptions break down. Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses requires a fundamentally different engineering approach, one that accounts for torque limitations, oxygen transfer rates, and shear sensitivity simultaneously. Key takeaways High-viscosity bioprocesses alter fluid dynamics in ways that standard mixing models underestimate. Rising culture viscosity reduces bulk flow velocity and creates stagnant zones that impair nutrient distribution and oxygen transfer, directly threatening cell viability and product quality. Impeller selection and configuration are the primary levers for managing mixing in dense, viscous cultures. Radial-flow and axial-flow impellers each offer distinct trade-offs between shear stress, power consumption, and bulk blending efficiency that must be matched to the specific culture system. The kLa value (the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient) is the practical benchmark for mixing adequacy in high-viscosity systems. Engineering teams that monitor and optimize kLa across scale can predict and prevent the oxygen limitation events that derail intensified runs. Why viscosity is the hidden variable in intensified bioprocessing Process intensification strategies (including high-density fed-batch, concentrated feeding regimens, and N-1 perfusion seed trains using alternating tangential flow filtration ) consistently push cultures toward rheological conditions that standard bioreactor mixing designs were never optimized to handle. As viable cell densities reach 40 to 80 million cells per milliliter in intensified fed-batch and continuous processes, and as concentrated glucose feeds and accumulated metabolites thicken the culture broth, fluid behavior shifts from Newtonian toward non-Newtonian, meaning viscosity itself becomes a dynamic variable that changes with shear rate, temperature, and fermentation stage. This rheological shift has direct consequences for bioreactor mixing performance. Research published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering on non-Newtonian rheology in suspension cell cultures has demonstrated that assuming Newtonian viscosity significantly underpredicts shear stress in stirred bioreactors, and that shear stress values in high-density cultures can exceed those required to alter genetic expression in common cell lines. The Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow) drops as viscosity rises, pushing the flow regime from turbulent toward transitional or even laminar. Homogeneous mixing, which relies on turbulent energy dissipation to blend nutrients and disperse oxygen bubbles throughout the vessel, becomes increasingly difficult to sustain without either increasing impeller speed or redesigning the mixing geometry entirely. Read More The result is a set of competing engineering pressures that define the core challenge of mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses. Higher agitation speed increases power draw and shear stress, which can damage fragile cells or aggregates. Lower agitation preserves cell integrity but risks the formation of dead zones where oxygen depletion and nutrient gradients accumulate. The mechanics of mass transfer failure in viscous cultures Oxygen transfer rate (OTR) is the first parameter to deteriorate as culture viscosity rises. Oxygen is sparingly soluble in aqueous culture medium, and its transfer from the gas phase into the liquid phase depends on the gas-liquid interfacial area and the liquid film mass transfer coefficient. Both are adversely affected by increased viscosity. Higher viscosity suppresses bubble rise velocity, promotes bubble coalescence into larger low-surface-area bubbles, and reduces the turbulent eddies that thin the liquid film around each bubble, all of which decrease the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa). The relationship between kLa and viscosity is well characterized in published bioprocess engineering literature. A 2025 study in Biotechnology Journal on CHO cell suspension rheology and its effects on high-density cultivation found a 10 to 40% decrease in the volumetric mass transfer coefficient as culture rheology shifted from water-like conditions. This means that a bioreactor running an intensified process may require substantially more agitation power to maintain the same dissolved oxygen (DO) setpoint compared to a standard lower-density fed-batch in the same vessel. Carbon dioxide removal presents a parallel and frequently underappreciated mass transfer challenge in high-viscosity cultures. CO₂ accumulation is a known inhibitor of cell growth and a driver of pH excursions, and its stripping from viscous broth is governed by similar mass transfer physics as oxygen absorption. Engineers designing agitation strategies for high-density cultures must account for both gas transfer directions simultaneously, which often means optimizing sparger design and gas flow rates alongside impeller configuration. Impeller selection and configuration for high-viscosity applications The impeller is the primary tool for delivering mechanical energy to the culture and generating the fluid motion that drives mixing and mass transfer. For high-viscosity bioprocesses, impeller selection cannot default to the configurations used in standard fed-batch processes. The choice between radial-flow impellers, such as Rushton turbines, and axial-flow impellers, such as pitched-blade or hydrofoil designs, involves trade-offs that become more consequential as viscosity rises. Radial-flow impellers generate strong turbulence and high local shear in the impeller discharge zone, which benefits gas dispersion and kLa but creates steep shear gradients that can damage shear-sensitive cells. Axial-flow impellers produce lower local shear with better bulk circulation, which is advantageous for maintaining culture homogeneity in large-volume or high-viscosity systems where flow circulation is the limiting factor rather than local turbulence. Many modern bioreactor designs for intensified processes use staged impeller configurations, combining a radial-flow lower impeller for gas dispersion with one or more axial-flow upper impellers for bulk mixing. CFD models solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion in three dimensions, accounting for the geometry of the vessel, impeller, and sparger, and can incorporate non-Newtonian rheological models to simulate the behavior of viscous culture broth. For bioreactor mixing challenges in high-viscosity processes, CFD modeling allows engineers to visualize flow fields, identify stagnant zones, and predict mixing times before a physical vessel is constructed or modified. The practical workflow typically begins with rheological characterization of the culture broth, construction of a three-dimensional vessel geometry model, and simulation of fluid flow across a range of agitation speeds and gas flow rates. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start. Oxygen enrichment must be implemented carefully because elevated local oxygen concentrations near the sparger can cause oxidative stress in cells close to the bubble formation zone. Achieving consistent homogeneity in intensified bioreactor mixing
Thicker, intensified cultures create bigger mass transfer problems, and only precise agitation keeps them in check. When cell densities climb and viscosity rises in fed-batch and perfusion processes, conventional mixing assumptions break down. Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses requires a fundamentally different engineering approach, one that accounts for torque limitations, oxygen transfer rates, and shear sensitivity simultaneously.
Key takeaways High-viscosity bioprocesses alter fluid dynamics in ways that standard mixing models underestimate. Rising culture viscosity reduces bulk flow velocity and creates stagnant zones that impair nutrient distribution and oxygen transfer, directly threatening cell viability and product quality. Impeller selection and configuration are the primary levers for managing mixing in dense, viscous cultures. Radial-flow and axial-flow impellers each offer distinct trade-offs between shear stress, power consumption, and bulk blending efficiency that must be matched to the specific culture system. The kLa value (the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient) is the practical benchmark for mixing adequacy in high-viscosity systems. Engineering teams that monitor and optimize kLa across scale can predict and prevent the oxygen limitation events that derail intensified runs.

Process intensification strategies (including high-density fed-batch, concentrated feeding regimens, and N-1 perfusion seed trains using alternating tangential flow filtration ) consistently push cultures toward rheological conditions that standard bioreactor mixing designs were never optimized to handle. As viable cell densities reach 40 to 80 million cells per milliliter in intensified fed-batch and continuous processes, and as concentrated glucose feeds and accumulated metabolites thicken the culture broth, fluid behavior shifts from Newtonian toward non-Newtonian, meaning viscosity itself becomes a dynamic variable that changes with shear rate, temperature, and fermentation stage.

This rheological shift has direct consequences for bioreactor mixing performance. Research published in Biotechnology and Bioengineering on non-Newtonian rheology in suspension cell cultures has demonstrated that assuming Newtonian viscosity significantly underpredicts shear stress in stirred bioreactors, and that shear stress values in high-density cultures can exceed those required to alter genetic expression in common cell lines. The Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in fluid flow) drops as viscosity rises, pushing the flow regime from turbulent toward transitional or even laminar. Homogeneous mixing, which relies on turbulent energy dissipation to blend nutrients and disperse oxygen bubbles throughout the vessel, becomes increasingly difficult to sustain without either increasing impeller speed or redesigning the mixing geometry entirely.

The result is a set of competing engineering pressures that define the core challenge of mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses. Higher agitation speed increases power draw and shear stress, which can damage fragile cells or aggregates. Lower agitation preserves cell integrity but risks the formation of dead zones where oxygen depletion and nutrient gradients accumulate.
Oxygen transfer rate (OTR) is the first parameter to deteriorate as culture viscosity rises. Oxygen is sparingly soluble in aqueous culture medium, and its transfer from the gas phase into the liquid phase depends on the gas-liquid interfacial area and the liquid film mass transfer coefficient. Both are adversely affected by increased viscosity. Higher viscosity suppresses bubble rise velocity, promotes bubble coalescence into larger low-surface-area bubbles, and reduces the turbulent eddies that thin the liquid film around each bubble, all of which decrease the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa).
The relationship between kLa and viscosity is well characterized in published bioprocess engineering literature. A 2025 study in Biotechnology Journal on CHO cell suspension rheology and its effects on high-density cultivation found a 10 to 40% decrease in the volumetric mass transfer coefficient as culture rheology shifted from water-like conditions. This means that a bioreactor running an intensified process may require substantially more agitation power to maintain the same dissolved oxygen (DO) setpoint compared to a standard lower-density fed-batch in the same vessel.

Carbon dioxide removal presents a parallel and frequently underappreciated mass transfer challenge in high-viscosity cultures. CO₂ accumulation is a known inhibitor of cell growth and a driver of pH excursions, and its stripping from viscous broth is governed by similar mass transfer physics as oxygen absorption. Engineers designing agitation strategies for high-density cultures must account for both gas transfer directions simultaneously, which often means optimizing sparger design and gas flow rates alongside impeller configuration.
The impeller is the primary tool for delivering mechanical energy to the culture and generating the fluid motion that drives mixing and mass transfer. For high-viscosity bioprocesses, impeller selection cannot default to the configurations used in standard fed-batch processes. The choice between radial-flow impellers, such as Rushton turbines, and axial-flow impellers, such as pitched-blade or hydrofoil designs, involves trade-offs that become more consequential as viscosity rises.
Radial-flow impellers generate strong turbulence and high local shear in the impeller discharge zone, which benefits gas dispersion and kLa but creates steep shear gradients that can damage shear-sensitive cells. Axial-flow impellers produce lower local shear with better bulk circulation, which is advantageous for maintaining culture homogeneity in large-volume or high-viscosity systems where flow circulation is the limiting factor rather than local turbulence. Many modern bioreactor designs for intensified processes use staged impeller configurations, combining a radial-flow lower impeller for gas dispersion with one or more axial-flow upper impellers for bulk mixing.

Impeller-to-vessel diameter ratio (D/T) is another variable that must be revisited for high-viscosity applications. Published engineering guidance for animal cell culture places the standard D/T range between 0.33 and 0.5, and moving toward the upper end of that range can significantly improve mixing time and reduce zone heterogeneity in viscous cultures. As culture viscosity rises, torque demand increases nonlinearly, so the mechanical drive system must be specified with adequate torque capacity, validated against the worst-case viscosity expected at peak cell density before committing to a vessel configuration.
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has moved from a research tool into a practical engineering resource for bioreactor scale-up, and its value is particularly high for high-viscosity applications where empirical correlations developed for low-viscosity systems can mislead. CFD models solve the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion in three dimensions, accounting for the geometry of the vessel, impeller, and sparger, and can incorporate non-Newtonian rheological models to simulate the behavior of viscous culture broth.
For bioreactor mixing challenges in high-viscosity processes, CFD modeling allows engineers to visualize flow fields, identify stagnant zones, and predict mixing times before a physical vessel is constructed or modified. Simulations of non-Newtonian fermentation broths can accurately predict mixing time increases relative to water-like conditions, with stagnant zone formation confirmable by tracer experiments in physical vessels. A mass-transfer modeling study in Biochemical Engineering Journal demonstrated that this approach enabled direct scale-up of a CHO antibody process from 2-L to 1,500-L without intermediate steps, with consistent process performance and product quality across scales.
Biochemical Engineering Journal
The practical workflow typically begins with rheological characterization of the culture broth, construction of a three-dimensional vessel geometry model, and simulation of fluid flow across a range of agitation speeds and gas flow rates. Connecting this approach to the broader framework of process intensification and continuous bioprocessing ensures that mixing decisions are integrated with upstream and downstream process constraints from the start.
process intensification and continuous bioprocessing
Maintaining dissolved oxygen above the critical threshold becomes progressively more difficult as culture viscosity rises and kLa declines. Setpoints commonly fall in the range of 20 to 60% air saturation for mammalian cell cultures, with working targets often set between 30 and 50%. The standard dissolved oxygen control cascade, which increases agitation speed and then increases airflow rate as DO falls, remains the primary control strategy but must be implemented with culture-specific limits to prevent shear damage or excessive CO₂ accumulation from high gas flow rates.
Oxygen enrichment of the inlet gas stream (substituting pure oxygen or high-oxygen mixtures for air) is a widely used supplemental strategy for maintaining DO in high-density, high-viscosity cultures. By increasing the partial pressure of oxygen in the sparged gas, enrichment increases the driving force for oxygen transfer across the gas-liquid interface without requiring a proportional increase in gas flow rate, which would otherwise strip CO₂ and drive pH excursions. Oxygen enrichment must be implemented carefully because elevated local oxygen concentrations near the sparger can cause oxidative stress in cells close to the bubble formation zone.

Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses? Bioreactor mixing in high-viscosity bioprocesses refers to the agitation strategies and engineering approaches used to maintain homogeneous culture conditions (including nutrient distribution, dissolved oxygen, and pH uniformity) when culture broth rheology departs from standard low-viscosity conditions due to high cell densities, concentrated feeds, or accumulated metabolites. Why does high cell density increase culture viscosity? Elevated cell density increases the volumetric fraction of suspended biomass in the culture medium and promotes the accumulation of extracellular proteins, polysaccharides, and metabolic byproducts that collectively raise apparent viscosity. Non-Newtonian rheological behavior emerges when these components interact with shear forces during agitation. How does viscosity affect oxygen mass transfer in bioreactors? Increased viscosity reduces the volumetric oxygen mass transfer coefficient (kLa) by promoting bubble coalescence, slowing bubble rise velocity, and thickening the liquid film resistance at the gas-liquid interface. The result is impaired oxygen supply to cells, which risks dissolved oxygen limitation and reduced cell productivity. News How magnetic particle imaging is giving cell therapy a navigation system Scientists at Johns Hopkins used a whole-body imaging technique to track where therapeutic cells go after injection Written by Andrea Corona Andrea Corona Andrea Corona is the senior editor at Drug Discovery News , where she leads daily editorial planning and produces original reporting on breakthroughs in drug discovery View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 2, 2026 | 3 min read Whole-body magnetic particle imaging (MPI) enables quantitative, noninvasive tracking of injected therapeutic cells across tissues, allowing researchers to compare how different injection routes affect delivery to target organs. Miranda Ansari Download PDF Cell therapies have transformed treatment for certain blood cancers and hold promise for autoimmune diseases and neurological conditions, but they share a fundamental problem: once therapeutic cells are injected into a patient, clinicians have almost no way to know where they go. Conventional imaging technologies including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) cannot reliably visualize the small cell numbers involved in these treatments, leaving researchers without feedback on whether a therapy is reaching its target, how many cells arrive, or why some patients respond and others do not. A study published in Science Advances from researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine describes a potential path toward solving that problem. Using magnetic particle imaging (MPI) — a newer imaging technology that detects magnetically labeled cells with high sensitivity and no tissue background signal — the team tracked two types of therapeutic cells across the whole body in living mice, comparing how injection route, cell size, dose, and disease state influenced biodistribution. The results suggest MPI could eventually provide the real-time, quantitative cell tracking that cell therapy development has so far lacked. In a press release , senior author Jeff Bulte , professor of radiology and radiological science and director of cellular imaging at the Johns Hopkins Institute for Cell Engineering, said that the work points toward using MPI to determine more precise cell therapy doses for individual patients. Read More What the imaging revealed The team labeled two cell types of different sizes — mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) at approximately 25 micrometers and neural precursor cells (NPCs) derived from induced pluripotent stem cells at approximately 10 micrometers — with superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) nanoparticles, then injected them into normal mice and mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a well-established preclinical model for multiple sclerosis (MS). MPI generates a positive signal proportional to the number of labeled cells present and is not attenuated by surrounding tissue — unlike MRI, which produces hypointense signals prone to artifacts and interference. That quantitative, whole-body readout allowed the team to assess cell distribution across multiple organs simultaneously without ionizing radiation or sacrificing the animal. The most significant finding concerned delivery route. Intra-arterial injection resulted in substantially more cells reaching target organs — the brain and spleen — compared with intravenous injection. In EAE mice, therapeutic cells accumulated in the spleen, an organ implicated in MS pathology. In the press release, lead author Ali Shakeri-Zadeh , assistant professor of radiology and radiological science at Johns Hopkins, noted that the spleen is thought to be a source of harmful immune T cells in MS, and that the accumulation of therapeutic cells there suggested they could engage disease activity directly at that site. The imaging also revealed off-target accumulation in the lungs and liver — relevant for biodistribution safety assessments. In normal mice, cells traveled to the lungs, liver, and brain, but were not detectable in the spleen, underscoring that disease state shaped organ distribution in ways healthy animal data alone could not predict. Why this matters for cell therapy development Dosing decisions for cell therapies are currently made with limited information about how many cells actually reach the intended site, conflating variability in delivery with variability in response. A quantitative imaging readout that decouples the two would allow developers to optimize injection routes, refine dose ranges, and identify sources of variability that make cell therapy outcomes difficult to predict or replicate. Previous work established MPI's utility for tracking adoptively transferred T cells in vivo in brain tumor models, showing that magnetic labeling does not impair cell function and that MPI can detect labeled cells after intravenous or intracerebroventricular delivery. The Johns Hopkins study extends that precedent across a broader range of cell types, delivery routes, and disease contexts. Human-scale MPI systems capable of brain imaging have been developed and validated in recent literature. As the technology moves toward clinical application, preclinical datasets like those generated here will be critical for interpreting what human MPI images of therapeutic cell distribution actually mean — and whether real-time imaging at the point of delivery can move cell therapy dosing toward the individualized model precision medicine requires. Whole-body magnetic particle imaging (MPI) enables quantitative, noninvasive tracking of injected therapeutic cells across tissues, allowing researchers to compare how different injection routes affect delivery to target organs. Miranda Ansari
Whole-body magnetic particle imaging (MPI) enables quantitative, noninvasive tracking of injected therapeutic cells across tissues, allowing researchers to compare how different injection routes affect delivery to target organs.
Miranda Ansari
Cell therapies have transformed treatment for certain blood cancers and hold promise for autoimmune diseases and neurological conditions, but they share a fundamental problem: once therapeutic cells are injected into a patient, clinicians have almost no way to know where they go. Conventional imaging technologies including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) cannot reliably visualize the small cell numbers involved in these treatments, leaving researchers without feedback on whether a therapy is reaching its target, how many cells arrive, or why some patients respond and others do not. A study published in Science Advances from researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine describes a potential path toward solving that problem. Using magnetic particle imaging (MPI) — a newer imaging technology that detects magnetically labeled cells with high sensitivity and no tissue background signal — the team tracked two types of therapeutic cells across the whole body in living mice, comparing how injection route, cell size, dose, and disease state influenced biodistribution. The results suggest MPI could eventually provide the real-time, quantitative cell tracking that cell therapy development has so far lacked. In a press release , senior author Jeff Bulte , professor of radiology and radiological science and director of cellular imaging at the Johns Hopkins Institute for Cell Engineering, said that the work points toward using MPI to determine more precise cell therapy doses for individual patients. Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More What the imaging revealed The team labeled two cell types of different sizes — mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) at approximately 25 micrometers and neural precursor cells (NPCs) derived from induced pluripotent stem cells at approximately 10 micrometers — with superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) nanoparticles, then injected them into normal mice and mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a well-established preclinical model for multiple sclerosis (MS). MPI generates a positive signal proportional to the number of labeled cells present and is not attenuated by surrounding tissue — unlike MRI, which produces hypointense signals prone to artifacts and interference. That quantitative, whole-body readout allowed the team to assess cell distribution across multiple organs simultaneously without ionizing radiation or sacrificing the animal. The most significant finding concerned delivery route. Intra-arterial injection resulted in substantially more cells reaching target organs — the brain and spleen — compared with intravenous injection. In EAE mice, therapeutic cells accumulated in the spleen, an organ implicated in MS pathology. In the press release, lead author Ali Shakeri-Zadeh , assistant professor of radiology and radiological science at Johns Hopkins, noted that the spleen is thought to be a source of harmful immune T cells in MS, and that the accumulation of therapeutic cells there suggested they could engage disease activity directly at that site. The imaging also revealed off-target accumulation in the lungs and liver — relevant for biodistribution safety assessments. In normal mice, cells traveled to the lungs, liver, and brain, but were not detectable in the spleen, underscoring that disease state shaped organ distribution in ways healthy animal data alone could not predict. Why this matters for cell therapy development Dosing decisions for cell therapies are currently made with limited information about how many cells actually reach the intended site, conflating variability in delivery with variability in response. A quantitative imaging readout that decouples the two would allow developers to optimize injection routes, refine dose ranges, and identify sources of variability that make cell therapy outcomes difficult to predict or replicate. Previous work established MPI's utility for tracking adoptively transferred T cells in vivo in brain tumor models, showing that magnetic labeling does not impair cell function and that MPI can detect labeled cells after intravenous or intracerebroventricular delivery. The Johns Hopkins study extends that precedent across a broader range of cell types, delivery routes, and disease contexts. Human-scale MPI systems capable of brain imaging have been developed and validated in recent literature. As the technology moves toward clinical application, preclinical datasets like those generated here will be critical for interpreting what human MPI images of therapeutic cell distribution actually mean — and whether real-time imaging at the point of delivery can move cell therapy dosing toward the individualized model precision medicine requires.

articles.title: Bio‑Techne and Refeyn close critical gap in bispecific antibody and biosimilar characterization
articles.text:
Industry Perspectives Bio‑Techne and Refeyn close critical gap in bispecific antibody and biosimilar characterization The integrated workflow combines icIEF fractionation and mass photometry, enabling simultaneous assessment of charge and size variants at single molecule resolution . Written by Bio-Techne Bio-Techne Bio-Techne View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Refeyn Refeyn Refeyn Ltd. specializes in the development, production, and distribution of mass photometry technologies for industry and academia. Mass photometry and macro mass photometry are unique bioanalytical technologies pioneered by Refeyn. By quantifying light scattering from particles in solution, mass photometry enables the measurement of molecular mass at the single-particle level while macro mass photometry enables simultaneous measurement of viral vector size and contrast (a proxy for mass). Spun out of Oxford University in 2018, the company aims to make its technology accessible to all in the scientific community, enabling users to achieve new and better outcomes. Refeyn has been recognized for its unique approach to biomolecular analysis through multiple awards, including the Royal Society of Chemistry Emerging Technologies Competition. Applications of mass photometry include: Characterization of samples of biomolecules and viral vectors, and analysis of protein oligomerization, biomolecular interactions, and macromolecular assemblies. Utilizing the novel technologies of mass photometry and macro mass photometry, Refeyn’s products are capable of accurate analysis of single particles in solution, in their native state, and without the need for labels, opening up new possibilities for bioanalytics. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 4, 2026 | 2 min read credit: Refeyn and Bio-Techne Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 2:00 MINNEAPOLIS and OXFORD, UK — June 4, 2026 — Bio‑Techne Corporation (NASDAQ: TECH), a global provider of life science tools, reagents and diagnostic products, and Refeyn, the pioneer in mass photometry technology, today announced a first‑of‑its‑kind integrated workflow for the characterization of charge and size variants in bispecific antibodies and biosimilars. By combining R&D Systems MauriceFlex imaged capillary isoelectric focusing (icIEF) fractionation system with Refeyn’s TwoMP mass photometry platform , researchers can directly correlate charge heterogeneity with molecular weight and aggregation at single‑molecule resolution in a streamlined four‑hour workflow. Bispecific antibodies are among the fastest-growing classes of biotherapeutics, but their structural complexity makes thorough characterization challenging. Incomplete characterization can delay development, increase manufacturing risk, and lead to costly late‑stage failures. The MauriceFlex system delivers high-resolution separation and fractionation of charge variants, a capability increasingly expected in regulatory submissions. However, analyzing the size and aggregation of individual charge fractions has historically been difficult due to the large sample requirements of traditional methods. The integrated workflow addresses this challenge directly by pairing icIEF fractionation with mass photometry. Charge variants are first separated using MauriceFlex, then analyzed on Refeyn’s TwoMP platform, which requires only nanogram‑level sample and reveals size distribution and aggregation at single‑molecule resolution. Together, the technologies enable direct characterization of aggregation and size within icIEF-resolved charge variants—an insight not accessible with standalone methods—reducing reliance on multiple tests and enabling faster, more efficient process development. “Bispecifics are the fastest growing segment within next‑generation antibodies, but they are very difficult to characterize. This approach directly addresses one of the biggest challenges by combining icIEF fractionation with mass photometry. Researchers can now interrogate charge and size variants together in a single workflow,” said Gerry Mackay , CEO of Refeyn. “Our customers are under intense pressure to develop and manufacture increasingly complex biologics faster and more efficiently. Enabling deeper characterization with less sample helps them reduce risk, control costs, and make better decisions earlier in development,” said Will Geist , President of  Protein Sciences Segment at Bio-Techne. In a joint webinar , scientists demonstrated the workflow using Mosunetuzumab‑axgb and a biosimilar, tracking size-related changes in the molecule across charge variant fractions under multiple conditions. An application note “ Characterizing charge and size variants of bispecific antibodies by icIEF fractionation and mass photometry ,” with full findings is also available. The workflow will also be presented at the American Society for Mass Spectrometry (ASMS) conference, taking place May 31 – June 4, 2026, in San Diego. See booth and poster details here. Mar 16, 2026 | 6 min read Single-particle analytics reveal hidden challenges in manufacturing advanced therapies. credit: istock.com/sutlafk Download PDF Hena Divanovic is an Application Scientist with a strong background in the development of cell and gene therapies. Credit: REFEYN Advanced gene and cell therapies hold transformative potential, but realizing that promise comes with unique and often underestimated challenges. Beyond the scientific complexity of designing effective modalities, the path from early development to commercial supply is shaped by decisions made long before large-scale manufacturing begins. Each choice — from platform adoption to process design and analytical strategy — can reverberate across the program, influencing efficiency, cost, and scalability. In a sector where manufacturing intricacies define the pace and economics of success, understanding the interplay between process, analytics, and product knowledge is essential. In a recent conversation with Hena Divanovic , an Application Scientist at Refeyn , DDN explored how emerging analytical tools, adaptive development strategies, and a deeper integration of manufacturing insight can help developers navigate the high-stakes landscape of advanced therapies, mitigating risk while accelerating progress toward patient access. Advanced gene therapies still carry very high entry and manufacturing costs. Which cost drivers are most underestimated early in development? One of the most underestimated cost drivers in advanced gene therapy development is not a single technical challenge, but the downstream consequences of early strategic decisions made purely for speed. Platform processes and rapid phase-appropriate manufacturing can create early momentum, yet when they are applied without sufficient product and process understanding, they often shift risk, rather than reducing it. The real costs appear later through process variability, inefficient tech transfer, repeated comparability work, underperforming batches, and delayed clinical timelines. Suboptimal outcomes rarely originate from one gap alone; they reflect fragmented chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) development, where analytics, manufacturability, and scalability evolve separately instead of as a unified strategy. Platform approaches remain powerful enablers, but they require scientific judgement, not blind adoption. In my view, sustainable acceleration comes from integrating product knowledge, process design, and analytical strategy early, enabling data-driven decisions that minimize re-development and protect long-term program value. In a field where manufacturing defines success, early development discipline is ultimately one of the strongest levers for cost control. Many manufacturing technologies used today were inherited from earlier biologic modalities. Where do these legacy approaches fall short when applied to complex biomolecules such as viral vectors or gene-editing systems? Unlike traditional biologics, these products carry inherent heterogeneity, instability, and a level of biological variability that does not scale in a linear or fully predictable way. Applying the same scale-up logic, simply increasing vessel size or equipment capacity, often fails to address the real bottlenecks, which are productivity limits, process sensitivity, and product fragility. Analytics is another area where legacy thinking persists. While we often measure familiar parameters, methods remain insufficiently standardized and may not fully capture critical quality attributes unique to these modalities. Emerging analytical technologies exist, but industry adoption can be slow due to regulatory conservatism and operational complexity. At the same time, viral vectors and gene-editing systems are far more susceptible to environmental conditions, meaning small process deviations can translate into significant yield loss or quality risk, something traditional biologics platforms were not designed to manage. Ultimately, the gap is not just technological but conceptual. Legacy processes assume control through scale and standardization, whereas these newer modalities require deeper process understanding, adaptive manufacturing strategies, and willingness to integrate new analytical and production technologies earlier. Without that shift, programs risk high capital investment without proportional gains in robustness, scalability, or cost efficiency. Scaling gene therapy remains particularly challenging. How much of that challenge is fundamentally a manufacturing problem, and how much is actually an analytical data problem? How well do we understand how the process shapes the product? With the right level of insight, individual unit operations can be leveraged strategically rather than simply scaled mechanically. Analytics is a critical asset, but only when it delivers reliable data that truly reflects what is happening during production. The challenge is not deciding whether scaling is a manufacturing or an analytical problem, it is recognizing where variability originates and applying the right risk-mitigation strategies. For example, persistent variability in a downstream step should trigger structured root cause analysis to determine whether the driver is process conditions, equipment performance, raw material variability, or the assay itself. Strong controls and integrated development allow teams to resolve both aspects together, ensuring optimization is guided by real process behavior rather than uncertain signals. In this field, scalability is less about bigger equipment and more about better decisions, and those only come when manufacturing insight and analytical confidence move together. What does “fit-for-purpose analytics” really mean in the context of advanced therapies, and how does it differ from traditional quality control approaches? Fit-for-purpose analytics in advanced therapies means that analytical strategies evolve as the product matures. Early in development, the goal is often to generate directional insight rather than fully validated datasets, which has significant implications for how assays are designed and implemented across the product lifecycle. Instead of applying legacy quality control (QC) frameworks too early, methods are built around the specific questions being asked, particularly for highly heterogeneous modalities where commercial standards or reference materials may not yet exist. At early stages, analytics should prioritize understanding potency, product composition, and how process changes influence quality, rather than enforcing strict release-style testing. As product and process knowledge increases, those same methods can mature into more robust QC assays. This differs from traditional biologics, where assays are often standardized and validated early to confirm consistency against well-defined attributes. In advanced therapies, analytics begin more exploratory and orthogonal, enabling scientists to build true product understanding before locking processes into rigid specifications. What is mass photometry, and what fundamentally distinguishes it from the analytical assays that advanced therapy developers have traditionally relied on? Mass photometry is a label-free, single-particle analytical technology that measures the mass of individual biomolecules and viral particles in solution by using light scattering. Unlike many traditional assays, it requires minimal sample preparation, does not rely on labelling, and requires only 10µL of sample, in contrast to analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC), which can require up to 1mL of highly concentrated material, enabling rapid, high-resolution measurements within minutes. What fundamentally distinguishes mass photometry from analytical approaches traditionally used in advanced therapies is the level of direct insight it provides. Conventional assays often rely on bulk measurements or indirect readouts, whereas mass photometry allows developers to observe heterogeneity at the single-particle level, for example, distinguishing empty, partially filled, full, or overfilled viral capsids. This high-resolution, rapid assessment enables faster process understanding and decision-making, making it particularly powerful for complex and heterogeneous modalities where traditional methods may lack resolution or speed. Do you see mass photometry primarily as a replacement for existing assays, or as an enabler that allows companies to ask new questions about their products? Advanced therapy development rarely progresses by simply replacing one assay with another. Instead, new technologies expand the scope of questions we can ask about complex and heterogeneous products. Mass photometry should therefore be seen primarily as an enabler rather than a substitute for existing analytics. By providing high-resolution mass distribution data within minutes, it shifts how early development and process understanding evolve, allowing teams to explore aspects of product heterogeneity that were previously difficult to observe. Industry Perspectives Bio‑Techne and Refeyn close critical gap in bispecific antibody and biosimilar characterization The integrated workflow combines icIEF fractionation and mass photometry, enabling simultaneous assessment of charge and size variants at single molecule resolution . Written by Bio-Techne Bio-Techne Bio-Techne View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Refeyn Refeyn Refeyn Ltd. specializes in the development, production, and distribution of mass photometry technologies for industry and academia. Mass photometry and macro mass photometry are unique bioanalytical technologies pioneered by Refeyn. By quantifying light scattering from particles in solution, mass photometry enables the measurement of molecular mass at the single-particle level while macro mass photometry enables simultaneous measurement of viral vector size and contrast (a proxy for mass). Spun out of Oxford University in 2018, the company aims to make its technology accessible to all in the scientific community, enabling users to achieve new and better outcomes. Refeyn has been recognized for its unique approach to biomolecular analysis through multiple awards, including the Royal Society of Chemistry Emerging Technologies Competition. Applications of mass photometry include: Characterization of samples of biomolecules and viral vectors, and analysis of protein oligomerization, biomolecular interactions, and macromolecular assemblies. Utilizing the novel technologies of mass photometry and macro mass photometry, Refeyn’s products are capable of accurate analysis of single particles in solution, in their native state, and without the need for labels, opening up new possibilities for bioanalytics. Jun 4, 2026 | 2 min read credit: Refeyn and Bio-Techne Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 2:00 MINNEAPOLIS and OXFORD, UK — June 4, 2026 — Bio‑Techne Corporation (NASDAQ: TECH), a global provider of life science tools, reagents and diagnostic products, and Refeyn, the pioneer in mass photometry technology, today announced a first‑of‑its‑kind integrated workflow for the characterization of charge and size variants in bispecific antibodies and biosimilars. By combining R&D Systems MauriceFlex imaged capillary isoelectric focusing (icIEF) fractionation system with Refeyn’s TwoMP mass photometry platform , researchers can directly correlate charge heterogeneity with molecular weight and aggregation at single‑molecule resolution in a streamlined four‑hour workflow. Bispecific antibodies are among the fastest-growing classes of biotherapeutics, but their structural complexity makes thorough characterization challenging. Incomplete characterization can delay development, increase manufacturing risk, and lead to costly late‑stage failures. The MauriceFlex system delivers high-resolution separation and fractionation of charge variants, a capability increasingly expected in regulatory submissions. However, analyzing the size and aggregation of individual charge fractions has historically been difficult due to the large sample requirements of traditional methods. The integrated workflow addresses this challenge directly by pairing icIEF fractionation with mass photometry. Charge variants are first separated using MauriceFlex, then analyzed on Refeyn’s TwoMP platform, which requires only nanogram‑level sample and reveals size distribution and aggregation at single‑molecule resolution. Together, the technologies enable direct characterization of aggregation and size within icIEF-resolved charge variants—an insight not accessible with standalone methods—reducing reliance on multiple tests and enabling faster, more efficient process development. “Bispecifics are the fastest growing segment within next‑generation antibodies, but they are very difficult to characterize. This approach directly addresses one of the biggest challenges by combining icIEF fractionation with mass photometry. Researchers can now interrogate charge and size variants together in a single workflow,” said Gerry Mackay , CEO of Refeyn. “Our customers are under intense pressure to develop and manufacture increasingly complex biologics faster and more efficiently. Enabling deeper characterization with less sample helps them reduce risk, control costs, and make better decisions earlier in development,” said Will Geist , President of  Protein Sciences Segment at Bio-Techne. In a joint webinar , scientists demonstrated the workflow using Mosunetuzumab‑axgb and a biosimilar, tracking size-related changes in the molecule across charge variant fractions under multiple conditions. An application note “ Characterizing charge and size variants of bispecific antibodies by icIEF fractionation and mass photometry ,” with full findings is also available. The workflow will also be presented at the American Society for Mass Spectrometry (ASMS) conference, taking place May 31 – June 4, 2026, in San Diego. See booth and poster details here. Credit: REFEYN Advanced gene and cell therapies hold transformative potential, but realizing that promise comes with unique and often underestimated challenges. Beyond the scientific complexity of designing effective modalities, the path from early development to commercial supply is shaped by decisions made long before large-scale manufacturing begins. Each choice — from platform adoption to process design and analytical strategy — can reverberate across the program, influencing efficiency, cost, and scalability. In a sector where manufacturing intricacies define the pace and economics of success, understanding the interplay between process, analytics, and product knowledge is essential. In a recent conversation with Hena Divanovic , an Application Scientist at Refeyn , DDN explored how emerging analytical tools, adaptive development strategies, and a deeper integration of manufacturing insight can help developers navigate the high-stakes landscape of advanced therapies, mitigating risk while accelerating progress toward patient access. Advanced gene therapies still carry very high entry and manufacturing costs. Which cost drivers are most underestimated early in development? One of the most underestimated cost drivers in advanced gene therapy development is not a single technical challenge, but the downstream consequences of early strategic decisions made purely for speed. Platform processes and rapid phase-appropriate manufacturing can create early momentum, yet when they are applied without sufficient product and process understanding, they often shift risk, rather than reducing it. The real costs appear later through process variability, inefficient tech transfer, repeated comparability work, underperforming batches, and delayed clinical timelines. Suboptimal outcomes rarely originate from one gap alone; they reflect fragmented chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) development, where analytics, manufacturability, and scalability evolve separately instead of as a unified strategy. Platform approaches remain powerful enablers, but they require scientific judgement, not blind adoption. In my view, sustainable acceleration comes from integrating product knowledge, process design, and analytical strategy early, enabling data-driven decisions that minimize re-development and protect long-term program value. In a field where manufacturing defines success, early development discipline is ultimately one of the strongest levers for cost control. Many manufacturing technologies used today were inherited from earlier biologic modalities. Where do these legacy approaches fall short when applied to complex biomolecules such as viral vectors or gene-editing systems? Unlike traditional biologics, these products carry inherent heterogeneity, instability, and a level of biological variability that does not scale in a linear or fully predictable way. Applying the same scale-up logic, simply increasing vessel size or equipment capacity, often fails to address the real bottlenecks, which are productivity limits, process sensitivity, and product fragility. Analytics is another area where legacy thinking persists. While we often measure familiar parameters, methods remain insufficiently standardized and may not fully capture critical quality attributes unique to these modalities. Emerging analytical technologies exist, but industry adoption can be slow due to regulatory conservatism and operational complexity. At the same time, viral vectors and gene-editing systems are far more susceptible to environmental conditions, meaning small process deviations can translate into significant yield loss or quality risk, something traditional biologics platforms were not designed to manage. Ultimately, the gap is not just technological but conceptual. Legacy processes assume control through scale and standardization, whereas these newer modalities require deeper process understanding, adaptive manufacturing strategies, and willingness to integrate new analytical and production technologies earlier. Without that shift, programs risk high capital investment without proportional gains in robustness, scalability, or cost efficiency. Scaling gene therapy remains particularly challenging. How much of that challenge is fundamentally a manufacturing problem, and how much is actually an analytical data problem? How well do we understand how the process shapes the product? With the right level of insight, individual unit operations can be leveraged strategically rather than simply scaled mechanically. Analytics is a critical asset, but only when it delivers reliable data that truly reflects what is happening during production. The challenge is not deciding whether scaling is a manufacturing or an analytical problem, it is recognizing where variability originates and applying the right risk-mitigation strategies. For example, persistent variability in a downstream step should trigger structured root cause analysis to determine whether the driver is process conditions, equipment performance, raw material variability, or the assay itself. Strong controls and integrated development allow teams to resolve both aspects together, ensuring optimization is guided by real process behavior rather than uncertain signals. In this field, scalability is less about bigger equipment and more about better decisions, and those only come when manufacturing insight and analytical confidence move together. Instead of applying legacy quality control (QC) frameworks too early, methods are built around the specific questions being asked, particularly for highly heterogeneous modalities where commercial standards or reference materials may not yet exist. At early stages, analytics should prioritize understanding potency, product composition, and how process changes influence quality, rather than enforcing strict release-style testing. As product and process knowledge increases, those same methods can mature into more robust QC assays. This differs from traditional biologics, where assays are often standardized and validated early to confirm consistency against well-defined attributes. In advanced therapies, analytics begin more exploratory and orthogonal, enabling scientists to build true product understanding before locking processes into rigid specifications. This high-resolution, rapid assessment enables faster process understanding and decision-making, making it particularly powerful for complex and heterogeneous modalities where traditional methods may lack resolution or speed.
